title: Adaption Labs: Gradient-Free Continual Learning — Sara Hooker, Adaption
talk_summary: Sara Hooker argues that pre-training scale has saturated and that the highest returns now come from post-training, inference-time, and data co-optimization, which lowers barriers to building capable models. She describes an 'Auto Scientist' system that co-optimizes data and model choices via automated search, outperforming human researchers on some model-training tasks.

takeaways.technique: Cheapest-capable-model selection over monolithic model use
takeaways.what_they_do: Argues against shipping one model to everyone and for spending compute proportional to task difficulty, with adaptive test-time compute per task.
takeaways.evidence_quote: most people intuitively understand that you shouldn't ship the same model to billions of people... it's not a particularly good use of compute

takeaways.what_they_do: Their auto-research loop only produced gains once they co-optimized data quality alongside model adaptation, rather than treating data as a separate agent decision.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we did not get the returns for like how much you can squeeze out of performance until you control for data quality

takeaways.what_they_do: An automated loop explores hyperparameter/config combinations humans are wary of changing all at once, exploiting a broad search space.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it changes a lot of the hyperparameters. Typically, that humans are much more wary about changing all at once

takeaways.technique: Shift spend from pre-training to post-training/inference
takeaways.what_they_do: Argues pre-training scale is saturated and returns now come from post-training and inference compute, which is more distributed and cheaper per FLOP.
takeaways.evidence_quote: pre-training size in particular is not your most lucrative axis of scale
